analysis.one_liner: Forces the Energy Department to begin taking nuclear plant waste by 1998 and builds an interim storage site in Nevada.
analysis.headline: Approved by the House Commerce Committee on a 30–4 vote and backed by 186 cosponsors from both parties, the bill sat on the House calendar from October 1995 and never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Nuclear utilities have paid a fee on every kilowatt-hour since 1982 for the government to take their spent fuel, but the Energy Department has no place to put it, so the waste keeps piling up at reactor sites. This bill orders DOE to start accepting the waste by January 31, 1998, builds a federal interim storage site at the Nevada Test Site, and directs a permanent repository at Yucca Mountain. To hit the deadline, it short-circuits environmental review of alternatives, blocks the EPA from setting its own radiation standard for the repository, limits courts' ability to halt construction, and offers Nevada payments while making clear that taking the money does not mean Nevada consents to the site.
analysis.who_benefits: Nuclear utilities, which get a guaranteed federal pickup date for spent fuel, a cap on the waste fee (1.0 mill per kilowatt-hour), remedies if DOE misses deadlines, and a link between waste contracts and reactor license renewals. Waste-handling, transport, and construction contractors gain mandated work, including a new rail corridor to the Nevada site. Reactor communities gain the promise of waste removal.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Energy to begin accepting spent nuclear fuel for interim storage no later than January 31, 1998, ending the open-ended wait utilities have faced since the 1982 law.

Caps the waste fee at an average of no more than 1.0 mill per kilowatt-hour of nuclear electricity through 2010 and thereafter, and lets a one-time payment free pre-1982 waste generators of further financial obligation.
Gives contract holders remedies if DOE fails to meet acceptance schedules, including DOE taking title to fuel left at the reactor site.
Ties NRC reactor license issuance and renewal to having a waste-disposal contract, formalizing the arrangement that supports continued reactor operation.

Offers Nevada and affected counties payments — $5 million a year to the state and $2.5 million to counties before fuel arrives, rising to $10 million and $5 million after first receipt — plus on-site oversight representatives and technical assistance.

analysis.who_pays: Nevada residents, who would host an interim storage facility at the Nevada Test Site without state consent; the bill waives environmental review of site alternatives and substitutes a congressionally set 100-millirem-per-year release standard for EPA's radiation protection standard. Federal taxpayers cover the share of storage and disposal costs attributable to defense waste. Ratepayers continue paying the waste fee. Courts and states lose leverage: the bill bars enjoining construction of the transport corridor or the storage facility before final licensing review.

drawbacks.text: The bill forbids the EPA from setting radiation release standards for the repository and sets its own 100-millirem annual dose standard, with licensing to be judged on it for the first 1,000 years and probabilistically to 10,000 years.

Environmental review is hollowed out: the environmental impact statements must not consider the need for the facilities, alternative sites, alternative routes, or alternative means of disposal, and route designation and site selection are exempted from review entirely.

No court may enjoin construction of the transportation corridor or operation of the interim storage facility before final review of the licensing decision, and Nevada's consultation rights stop short of a veto — accepting Nevada's benefits payments is expressly not consent.

Appropriations from the Nuclear Waste Fund are exempt from annual apportionment and from budget enforcement limits, and defense waste costs are allocated to the federal government, shifting some cost to general taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill addressed was real: utilities and their customers had paid into the Nuclear Waste Fund for over a decade while waste accumulated at reactor sites. But the bill bought speed by stripping the safeguards that normally shape a project of this kind — no site alternatives considered, no EPA radiation standard, no injunctions before licensing review, and no state veto. Whether a 1998 acceptance deadline was achievable was doubtful given that no site was licensed. It was a heavily one-sided bargain in favor of the waste generators, with Nevada absorbing the siting burden and the public losing normal environmental and judicial checks.

outcome.mechanism: The Commerce Committee approved it 30–4 and it was placed on the House calendar in October 1995, but no floor vote was ever scheduled before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Representative Fred Upton introduced the bill on February 23, 1995; it drew 186 cosponsors, 120 Republicans and 66 Democrats.
The Energy and Power Subcommittee forwarded it amended on a 18–2 vote in July 1995, and the full Commerce Committee ordered it reported 30–4 on August 2, 1995.
The committee-reported version was placed on the Union Calendar on October 24, 1995.
DOE submitted executive comment on January 11, 1996, and the bill received no further action; Congress adjourned on January 3, 1997 without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nevada and anyone relying on the standard environmental and radiation-safety rules kept protections the bill would have removed. Nuclear utilities gained nothing — they continued to store waste on-site and press claims against DOE for the government's missed deadlines.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nevada; utilities stayed stuck with on-site waste

for.name: Fred Upton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and promoted it through 1995 and 1996.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Approved the amended bill on a 30–4 vote and reported it to the House on September 20, 1995.

for.name: 186 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including 100 additional sponsors added the day it hit the calendar.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled floor consideration after the bill was placed on the Union Calendar in October 1995.

against.name: Clinton administration
against.what_they_did: Submitted formal comment on the bill and opposed legislation forcing an interim waste facility on Nevada over the state's objection, threatening vetoes of similar nuclear waste bills.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 120 Republicans and 66 Democrats cosponsored, and the Commerce Committee reported it 30–4; the obstruction came not from a party bloc but from the bill never reaching the floor.

industries.note: The bill guarantees a federal pickup date for spent fuel, caps the waste fee, and ties reactor license renewals to waste contracts, locking in the industry's operating model and its government-backed waste channel. Ratepayers fund that system through the fee, while Nevada hosts the facility and standard environmental and radiation protections are weakened to make it happen.

industries.industry: Nuclear waste transport and storage contractors
industries.note: The bill requires DOE to use private industry for waste transport 'to the fullest extent possible' and directs prompt licensing of private interim storage installations, creating mandated business. Public benefit depends on whether the weakened oversight of these operations is worth the convenience to reactor communities.

The bill mandates construction of a rail corridor from Lincoln County, Nevada to the storage site, plus heavy-haul road upgrades — a large construction program funded from the Nuclear Waste Fund. Local governments like Caliente receive replacement land and wastewater facilities.
